Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\geq 2$ and let $S^4=\mathbb R^4\cup\{\infty\}$ be the one-point compactification, oriented so the coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3,x^4$ on $\mathbb R^4$ have $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4>0$. Give $S^4$ a smooth round metric in the conformal class of the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^4$. A framed $U(N)$ connection is a smooth unitary connection $A$ on a Hermitian rank-$N$ vector bundle $E\to S^4$, together with a chosen unitary frame $\Phi:E_\infty\to\mathbb C^N$ of its fiber at $\infty$. Gauge transformations are smooth unitary bundle automorphisms that equal the identity in this frame at $\infty$. The curvature is $F_A$, and the Hodge operator is defined by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ on two-forms. Set $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2$ and $F_A^-=(F_A-*_gF_A)/2$; the anti-self-dual condition is $F_A^+=0$, and the self-dual condition is $F_A^-=0$.

Let $\mathfrak u(N)$ be the anti-Hermitian matrices and put $B_N(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_N(XY)$. In the trace convention of the library, the charge of $A$ is $q_N(A)=(8\pi^2)^{-1}\int_{S^4}B_N(F_A\wedge F_A)$, and the positive anti-self-dual instanton number is $k(A)=-q_N(A)$. For $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, the framed anti-self-dual charge-$k$ moduli set $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}$ consists of framed pairs $(E,A)$ with $F_A^+=0$ and $k(A)=k$, modulo the stated based gauge transformations. The integer-charge condition is part of the selected bundle sector; no analytic existence or uniqueness assertion is included in this definition. The trace and Hodge conventions agree with the supplied compact-four-manifold definition of $q_B$; its special $SU(2)$ integrality clause is not used to assert $U(N)$ integrality.

For $k\geq0$, take Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$. The ADHM data are
$$B_1,B_2\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),\qquad I\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V),\qquad J\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W).$$
Their data space is $\mathcal R_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W)$, and their complex and real moment-map expressions are
$$\mu_{\mathbb C}=[B_1,B_2]+IJ\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V).$$
Here $[X,Y]=XY-YX$, and $\dagger$ is the Hermitian adjoint. The two displayed formulas define maps $\mu_{\mathbb C}:\mathcal R_{k,N}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ and $\mu_{\mathbb R}:\mathcal R_{k,N}\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$, where $\mathcal R_{k,N}$ is the stated product of four Hom spaces and $\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ is the real vector space of Hermitian endomorphisms. They are the complex and real ADHM moment-map expressions, with these formulas fixing their normalization. A datum is stable when
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w):m\geq0,\ i_j\in\{1,2\},\ w\in W\}=V,$$
where the word of length zero is the identity. Equivalently, no proper $B_1,B_2$-invariant subspace of $V$ contains $\operatorname{im}I$. The group $GL(V)$ consists of invertible complex-linear endomorphisms, and $U(V)$ is its subgroup preserving the chosen Hermitian inner product. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. For $\zeta>0$, the stable complex ADHM quotient $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{GIT},\zeta}_{k,N}$ is the geometric quotient of $\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \text{stable}\}$ by $GL(V)$ in the positive stability chamber; $\zeta$ labels that chamber and is not an additional coordinate on the complex equation set.

For a real parameter $\zeta\geq0$, the real moment-map presentation is the quotient of $\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta\,\mathrm{id}_V,\ \text{stable}\}$ by $U(V)$. At $\zeta>0$ this is called the resolved or positive-FI ADHM quotient; at $\zeta=0$ its affine completion includes the small-instanton locus. The equations and quotient are definitions; this item does not assert that the real moment-map quotient is isomorphic to the stable complex quotient or to an instanton moduli space.

Write $\mathbb{CP}^2$ for the complex projective plane, $\ell_\infty=\{[0:z_1:z_2]\}$ for its line at infinity, and $\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}$ for the sheaf of holomorphic functions on that line. The affine chart $\mathbb{CP}^2\setminus\ell_\infty$ is $\mathbb C^2$; projective compactification adds the whole line $\ell_\infty$, unlike the one-point compactification $S^4$. Let $\mathcal O(1)$ be the hyperplane line bundle and $\mathcal O(m)=\mathcal O(1)^{\otimes m}$ for $m\geq0$. A coherent sheaf is a sheaf of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb{CP}^2}$-modules that is locally finitely presented; it is torsion-free when no nonzero local section is annihilated by a nonzero local function. Its rank is the dimension of its generic fiber over the function field. Define its Hilbert polynomial by $P_E(m)=\sum_{i=0}^2(-1)^i\dim_{\mathbb C}H^i(\mathbb{CP}^2,E\otimes\mathcal O(m))$ for all sufficiently large integers $m$. The framed Gieseker moduli space $\mathcal G_{k,N}$ is the moduli of pairs $(E,\Phi)$ with $E$ a rank-$N$ torsion-free coherent sheaf, $P_E(m)=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$, and $\Phi:E|_{\ell_\infty}\cong\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}^{\oplus N}$. Its locally-free locus is distinguished from the boundary of non-locally-free sheaves. The Uhlenbeck set-theoretic compactification is the disjoint union of strata $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k-\ell,N}\times\operatorname{Sym}^{\ell}(\mathbb R^4)$ for $0\leq\ell\leq k$, where $\operatorname{Sym}^{\ell}(\mathbb R^4)=(\mathbb R^4)^\ell/S_\ell$ records ideal point defects. The Gieseker space and the Uhlenbeck space are distinct: the former retains torsion-free sheaf data at the small-instanton boundary, while the latter records only ideal points. No compactness of either full space is asserted here.

Write $z_1=x^1+ix^2$ and $z_2=x^3+ix^4$. The compact torus $T=(S^1)^2\times T_G$, with $T_G\subset U(W)$ the diagonal framing torus, acts on ADHM data by
$$(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ).$$
This convention makes $\mu_{\mathbb C}$ transform with character $t_1t_2$ and leaves $\mu_{\mathbb R}$ invariant. Let $e_\alpha$ denote the character of the dual of the $\alpha$th framing line, so the framing representation has character $\mathbf W=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\mathbf W^\vee=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N e_\alpha$. For the rotation characters write $t_1,t_2$, and write $\epsilon_i=c_1^T(t_i)$ and $a_\alpha=c_1^T(e_\alpha)$ for their additive equivariant weights.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

A smooth action of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $M$ is **free** if
$G_x=\{e\}$ for every $x\in M$.

It is **proper** if its action-graph map

$$\Theta:G\times M\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Theta(g,x)=(g\cdot x,x),$$

is proper: $\Theta^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact
$K\subseteq M\times M$. The reversed coordinate convention
$(x,g\cdot x)$ is equivalent by the factor-swap homeomorphism. Freeness and
properness are independent conditions; neither is encoded by the other.

If a Lie group $G$ acts smoothly, freely, and properly on a smooth manifold
$M$, then the orbit space $M/G$ with its quotient topology is a Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold of dimension
$\dim M-\dim G$. It has a unique smooth structure for which the quotient map
$q:M\to M/G$ is a smooth surjective submersion.

For a smooth free proper action and $x\in M$, the quotient differential is
surjective and

$$\ker(dq_x)=T_x(G\cdot x).$$

Consequently it induces a canonical linear isomorphism

$$T_xM/T_x(G\cdot x)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }T_{[x]}(M/G).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Affine schemes equipped with open subschemes and isomorphisms on overlaps
satisfying the identity and cocycle conditions glue to a scheme, uniquely up to
unique isomorphism; the given affine schemes become an open affine cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group acting algebraically on a classical
variety $X$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]],
[[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). A $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to Y$ is a **categorical quotient** if every $G$-invariant morphism
$f:X\to Z$ of classical varieties factors uniquely as $f=\varphi\circ\pi$ with
$\varphi:Y\to Z$ a morphism.

It is a **geometric quotient** (Brion Definition 1.18) if

(i) $\pi$ is surjective and its fibres are exactly the $G$-orbits,

(ii) a subset $U\subseteq Y$ is open if and only if $\pi^{-1}(U)$ is open in
$X$, and

(iii) for every open $U\subseteq Y$ the pullback of regular functions is an
isomorphism $\mathcal O_Y(U)\to\mathcal O_X(\pi^{-1}(U))^G$ onto the
$G$-invariant regular functions on the preimage.

A geometric quotient is a categorical quotient and is unique up to unique
isomorphism; when it exists its underlying topological space is the orbit space
$X/G$ with the quotient topology. For an affine $G$-variety $X$ whose invariant
algebra $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is finitely generated, the affine model is the morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ induced by the inclusion
$\mathbb C[X]^G\subseteq\mathbb C[X]$. For a reductive $G$, the theorem below
proves this finite generation and makes the model a categorical quotient with
one closed orbit in each fibre
([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]).

**Why a geometric quotient is categorical.** Let $\pi:X\to Y$ satisfy (i)–(iii)
and let $f:X\to Z$ be a $G$-invariant morphism to a classical variety $Z$. By
(i) two points of a fibre of $\pi$ lie in one orbit, on which $f$ is constant,
so $f$ factors through a unique set map $\bar f:Y\to Z$. For $W\subseteq Z$
open, $\pi^{-1}(\bar f^{-1}(W))=f^{-1}(W)$ is open in $X$ by continuity of $f$,
so $\bar f^{-1}(W)$ is open in $Y$ by (ii): $\bar f$ is continuous. If $V$ is an
affine chart of $Z$ with coordinates $s$ and $U:=\bar f^{-1}(V)$, then
$s\circ f$ is a $G$-invariant regular function on $\pi^{-1}(U)$, hence by (iii)
is the pullback along $\pi$ of a unique regular function on $U$; that function
is $s\circ\bar f$. Since this holds for every coordinate $s$ of an affine chart,
$\bar f$ is a morphism
([[def-classical-affine-variety-morphism]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and local
agreement of the resulting morphisms on overlapping charts gives a morphism
$Y\to Z$. Surjectivity in (i) makes the factorisation unique. If also
$\pi':X\to Y'$ is a categorical quotient, the universal property applied to
$\pi'$ and to $\pi$ yields morphisms $\varphi:Y\to Y'$ with $\varphi\pi=\pi'$
and $\psi:Y'\to Y$ with $\psi\pi'=\pi$; then $(\varphi\psi)\pi'=\pi'$ and
$(\psi\varphi)\pi=\pi$, so uniqueness of the factorisation of $\pi'$ through
$\pi'$ and of $\pi$ through $\pi$ forces $\varphi\psi=\operatorname{id}_{Y'}$
and $\psi\varphi=\operatorname{id}_Y$. Thus categorical and geometric
quotients are unique up to unique isomorphism, and for a geometric quotient
(i)–(ii) say exactly that the underlying map is the quotient map of the orbit
equivalence relation with the quotient topology.

**Conventions.** This is the classical notion of Brion Definition 1.18 and the
paragraph after Theorem 1.24. The scheme-theoretic fppf quotient sheaf on the
AG-ACT-1 page is a different object and is not identified with this classical
notion here. In the classical register, $\operatorname{Spec}$ of a finitely
generated reduced complex algebra denotes its associated affine variety of
complex closed points with the classical regular-function sheaf; no
identification with the space of every scheme prime is used. For empty $X$ the
coordinate algebra is zero and its quotient is empty; finite generation and the
universal properties below are then immediate and fibre assertions are vacuous.
The definition itself uses no Axiom of Choice; the finite-generation theorem
referred to above inherits AC from its own named suppliers, so consumers of that
theorem carry AC, while nothing in this definition does.

Steps 2.1 and 5.1: k=0 has the empty moment and deformation equations.
Steps 1.1 and 5.1: N=1 uses the displayed finite-dimensional equations directly; k=1 needs only length-zero word frames.
